All of these issues pertain to the full DED leadership. This is the DED for programmes on data. It's the DED for humanitarian and supply chain on the reset and on the integrated supply chain. It is the DED management on efficiency, common back-office structures, shared services, and of course, under the leadership of our Executive Director. What you see here and someone referred to, 'We don't just want you to commit, we want you to see it doing.' Well, this is doing in action. This requires all hands on deck, and you have all these hands on deck, and I'll ask my colleagues, particularly with the many questions on the integrated supply chain and the reset, I'll ask Ted also to come in. And when I say this is the commitment of the entire higher leadership in action. Don't take my word for it, but I'll ask you to reflect on what the USG Guy Ryder said when we had the previous board, and he sat on this podium, and he actually said it: 'UNICEF doesn't just lean in, UNICEF leads on reform,' because we know that if UN reform works, all of us can deliver better for children. And that is why we are here. On the issue— I'll take a few issues, if I may, on where FFI is related or different from UN@80. Our colleague from Germany asked the question, as well as our colleague from El Salvador. They are different, but they're very aligned. FFI is our internal transformation process. It is how we are more efficient, how we do faster, largely, but not exclusively, in response to funding shortfalls. But it's a business transformation for UNICEF. UN at 80 is a whole-of-system approach, how the entire system can deliver more effectively and efficiently. Now, very clearly, these are aligned, but they're not 100% the same, not in their governance,, and not in their metrics of success. The work on the FFI is not mandated, for example, by UN@80 and actually preceded UN@80, but very clearly the idea that we need to be more effective, more efficient, and more coherent, both internally and as UNICEF with the wider UN system, that is what guides both processes, even if they are different. I'd like to recognize also the reference that was made in one of the interventions to Resolution 72/279 on the mandates of the different entities, including the Resident Coordinator. And this is a really important one. We are fully committed to the Resident Coordinator. We know that we have to do better, including as UNICEF, in terms of how we coordinate and how we synergize. It's not just coordination, it's how we synergize across the system. At the same time, we do not need additional bureaucratic layers. We cannot be slowed down in urgent times for children. We will have to retain direct access to ministries that we work with, whether it is on child rights, for example, with the Ministry of Labour, with Health, with Education, with Child Protection, but also with Finance. Because we also have a normative mandate, not just a programmatic mandate. The value of the RC really is the strategic coordination. And let me then perhaps look at my own experience, having done this work hands-on in 2005 to 2009 at country level in Vietnam, where the issue really was that we had about 8 agencies working on HIV/AIDS without them knowing it from each other in the same province, from UNICEF to UNFPA to UNAIDS to UNDP to FAO weaving HIV/AIDS prevention messages in agricultural extension. The issue is not per se that we all do it. The issue is that we're not informed, that we're burdening our local counterparts in the government and that we don't synergize across the system. That is what UN@80 should absolutely do. That's what we are fully committed to realize. For that, we will, however, have to look at how we do that, and there is— the CPD remains a key role. There is no competition between the cooperation framework and a CPD. A CPD is our accountability to you here in this forum as member states, from donors to recipient governments, in terms of how we allocate, what we allocate for, and how we measure results. If we break that by not having that, you will miss more than I think we can account for in monetary terms. Thank you. On information notes, we're very happy, of course, to provide the member states with additional informals or information notes. That is never a problem. And I would also perhaps in the spirit, if I may, of UN reform, very much appreciate the proposal from South Africa to see if we can perhaps combine the two agenda items. As said, they are very aligned. And so warm support to combine the items of UN OES reform and UN@80 in the future should the member states so decide. I'll keep it brief in the interest of time. Over to Mandip.

Okay, thank you, Kitty. So just to complement, I think, three things, and before I get to that, on the information note, because this issue was also tabled at our informal a couple of weeks ago. I think we were very clear-eyed about this. We didn't want to and we don't want to get ahead of the Secretary-General's-led UNAT initiative, so we were refraining from circulating reports from— and information notes from our end. But that being said, I mean, I think we are open to consideration and in and hope that this is coherent with your ask of other sister agencies as well, and that the Secretariat is in full awareness of this. I also want to acknowledge, if I may, our Global Directors in the room that are leading as well the shared services, Mark Petty, as well as Leila Pakala on the supply chain, and I'm sure they would join me in being very happy to have any follow-up specific discussions since there was a lot of interest on these issues, specific issues. I just— the first point I wanted to make is to Franz, and actually it was also highlighted by a couple of other board members around the important but difficult questions around country configuration, how do we streamline, how do we rationalize the presence, etc. And in this regard, we were forward-leaning by sharing some global parameters that could pragmatically help us to steer the process. And again, we are open to discussing these together with the rest of the system and the Secretariat so that we can advance in very practical terms. On France, we are absolutely with you in terms of support to the RC system, as you've heard both from DED, Kitty and me. I do want to just make one clarification. The RC's value is the strategic coordination, but it's not program delivery, because you had mentioned about guarantor of programmatic implementation, and this is where we need a lot of clarity and complementarity of roles and accountability. I think that— Thank you. This is already happening to a large extent in most contexts. We do it in a complementary way where the coordinator sticks to coordination. The operational agencies mandated by you as member states are in charge of program delivery. Again, happy to discuss this as a follow-on. The second point is on the sequencing, which was tabled by Germany on behalf— in your joint statement. Thank you for bringing up this important issue. Issue. I mean, on this one, maybe two things to say. First is, just to get practical about it, if we look at the whole universe of UN cooperation frameworks and CPDs from the agencies, funds, and programs lens, or from UNICEF lens, I would say that roughly around 5 to 10%, we find exceptional situations where the ideal sequencing is not happening in practice. So I do want to bring this reality check that in majority of the cases, we sequence it. We make sure that the cooperation frameworks are green-lighted at the country level, signed off, because that is the collective strategic direction of the UN system's work. And then the CPDs or equivalent programming instruments come to the governance bodies. Thank you. But in that, in those exceptional 5 to 10% cases where there is a war, a sudden onset of war, where there's a major crisis, a hurricane, and delays are caused in the signing off of the cooperation framework, and in a situation where the CPDs have already, which have been green-lighted by the national government as well as by the RCs, have made it to the board, In these situations, we are really counting on your support for pragmatic flexibility because the bottom line is that— is that of the substantive meaningful alignment which we spoke about in the earlier session. And in this regard, I mean, for the sequencing and aligning, we are paying very careful attention to some practical steps in terms of how we are engaging in the common country assessment, which is the evidence base that then allows us to determine what the priorities are in line with the national priorities. And similarly, in that regard, the strategic prioritization exercise that happens at the country level, we all actively engage in that for the cooperation framework, and based on that, we derive the country program documents. So again, Happy to engage further, and I thank Türkiye, El Salvador, as well as Eritrea for emphasizing the importance of program country ownership, but also operational flexibility in this regard. The third and final point, I think, on the regional reset, it was posed by the Russian Federation. I think this is probably one of the work packages where work The work is in progress. It's in the works, if you will. We don't have the clarity on all the aspects and the specific questions you have asked. That being said, two things from our side. The first is the regional reset should really help country teams to access specialized expertise that may not be available locally in country. For example, around the political economy analysis, foresight, climate data, and digital transformation, as well as looking at some of the cross-border specific initiatives or sub-regional challenges. And we are very keen to engage in, in what this would look like. And the second point is just building on some of the good practices and some of the not so good practices around instruments of channeling this assistance. There is talk about the Regional Collaborative Platform to upgrade it, to promote more cross-pillar synergy and coherence. In this regard, we have our Centers of Excellence and a very practical TA Hub tool, which we hope can also be leveraged in this. The bottom line is we do need clarity on governance arrangements, and to make sure that we are not duplicating the agency mechanisms and harnessing the comparative advantages at the regional level to the fullest. Thank you very much, and Madam President, it's back to you— actually, to Dede Ted.

Thank you very much, Madam President. Thank you for the different questions and comments. Let me quickly go through a few of the issues that related to the humanitarian supply function. Firstly, I think El Salvador asked about how all the different reform efforts relate to each other, and just in terms of the Humanitarian Reset and how it relates to UNHCR Humanitarian Cluster, the Humanitarian Reset predated also the UNHCR initiative, but they inform each other. Humanitarian Reset includes all of the IASC members, so it includes all of the major NGO networks, and what we're also striving to do on the UN80 side is make sure that as initiatives grow and they go to scale— to the EU's question— they are available, can be made available to some of our NGO partners as well, even though they've started as UN initiatives. So again, the idea is for them to inform each other and build on each other. Both France and Australia asked questions about how we're going to measure progress when it comes to the integrated supply chain initiative. And there will be a number of indicators that will be developed. They're not yet finalized, but it's issues like global delivery time reduced, lower prices for commodities, global transport and shipments, reduced fragmentation for in-country— —logistics. Logistics, and again, last mile delivery times that are more effective and faster, and then faster customs clearances, reducing demurrage costs, as well as lower costs in warehousing. So these are among the metrics that will be worked on and finalized and available and against which the initiative can be measured. Australia asked how we're working with with different agencies, in particular mentioned WFP and UNFPA. WFP is obviously a core co-sponsor of the initiative with us and UNDOS. In the case of UNFPA, we've had detailed discussions about how to divide labor and ensure complementarity on the procurement and distribution of maternal, newborn, and child health commodities and worked through 68 of the 84 categories of procurement and we'll get to the finish line on the remaining. The EU asked about going to scale and there, let me perhaps speak to the three components of the initiative, the Integrated Demand and Supply Chain Initiative. By definition, when we look at categories of supplies and when we reach agreement, which in some cases we're far along in reaching agreement on which agency will procure what category of supply, that will become an asset and an efficiency that's available beyond the pilot countries and indeed beyond humanitarian environment, because if, let's say, HCR and IOM are procuring relief supplies for the system as a whole, and UNICEF is procuring most categories of health supplies for the system as a whole, then those procurement contracts will become available not just for humanitarian settings, but beyond humanitarian settings. Similarly, for the kind of piggybacking that's taking place when it comes to global logistics and freight and shipping. So the global freight contracts, for example, that UNICEF and WFP have helped pull together are now being used by 33 agencies. The insurance services that UNICEF brokered are being used by 7 other agencies, and the more agencies use those services, the more the impact is at scale and global. For in-country logistics, it starts with the 5 countries mentioned, but the commitment is to move beyond the 5 countries before the end of the year. And then let me segue to a question also by the EU about localization, and there's many aspects of the reform that will promote localization, but I think a very important— and again, it's part of a more thoughtful, expanded definition of localization— will be a focus on local procurement and local manufacturing. And this is something that goes beyond the UN80 integrated supply chain proposal, but nonetheless is in that spirit. And part of what we're making the case for in the context of both the humanitarian reform, but also in in the context of UN80, is for much more procurement steps and manufacturing steps that benefit local economies rather than procurement that is done internationally. So as local as possible again when it comes to procurement. Finally, in the same vein as as what Mandeep offered. In the room today, we've got Leila Pakala, the Director of Supply Division, and we also have Mandeep— sorry, we have Lucia Almi, the Director of our Emergency Division, and they both would be more than happy to provide informal briefings on these issues. I think these are critical points where we could get into more detail and have more of an interactive exchange. Thank you.

Thank you. Are there further comments on this side? No? If not, I sincerely thank the Secretariat for their remarks. This is an extensive issue, and if there are no additional comments from the room, we shall consider the update on the UNAT initiative and implementation by UNICEF later later in the session under agenda item 19, the adoption of draft decisions. Now time has run out for us today and we will continue other items on our agenda next— in our next meeting tomorrow morning. Before we adjourn for the day, I believe that the Secretary of the Executive Board, Mr. Andrés Franco, would like to make an announcement.

Yes, thank you, Madame Chair. We will have the informal consultations of the informal draft decisions starting in 15 minutes in the Maurice Pate Room of the UNICEF House. And one of the reasons is you'll notice that one of the screens is not working, so they need to fix it, so we might as well just move there and get some work done. And 15 minutes should be pretty reasonable for I invite everybody to be there. I'm just checking with Ghete if that's okay. So, good. So, see you very soon at the UNICEF house.
I thank the Secretary for this announcement. Meeting is adjourned.
